items.title: A range as a quote
items.prose: The interviewer trades 20 against your range. They sell at your low end if the truth is below it, and buy at your high end if above. Width 2 to 12.
items.question: Finish both turns without losing money, and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: How many primes are there below 200? Quote your 90% range for 20. A width of 12 at most.
A hint: 25 of them are below 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A range that misses is traded against.

byKey.low: A range missed and the interviewer traded 20 against you. Primes thin out, so doubling the 25 below 100 overshoots.
byKey.crossed: Your low end met or passed your high end.

explain.text: There are 46 primes below 200. The model's 38 to 50 and 40 to 52 both hold it. Doubling the 25 below 100 gives 50 to 60, which is sold 20 at 50 twice: −£160.

items.question: What is the upper end of the 90% range? Give 2 places.

explain.text: $1.645 \times 5 = 8.22$, so the range is 51.78 to 68.22. Each tail holds 5%. The truth should land outside once in ten.

items.prose: A 90% range of 100 to 140. The truth is 95.
items.question: What does the range score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Width plus 20 times the miss.

byKey.width: You scored the width alone. The truth is 5 below.

explain.text: Width 40 plus 20 times the miss of 5 gives 140. A range of 90 to 140 would have scored 50. Ten more units of width would have saved 90.

items.prose: Dealer X offers 20.0 for 3 and 20.2 for 5. Dealer Y bids 20.4 for 4 and 20.1 for 6.
items.question: Buying from X and selling to Y, what profit can you lock, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match 3 at 20.0 and then 1 at 20.2 against Y's 4 at 20.4.

byKey.first: You stopped after X's first level. One more unit at 20.2 still sells at 20.4.
byKey.all: You kept going into Y's 20.1 bid, below X's 20.2.

explain.text: 3 at 20.0 and 1 at 20.2 fill Y's 4 at 20.4: £1.20 + £0.20. X's next offer, 20.2, is above Y's next bid, 20.1. Four units for £1.40.

items.prose: A bookmaker offers evens, 4 to 1 and 4 to 1 on three outcomes. Exactly one of them happens.
items.question: Staking so each bet returns £10, what do you lock in, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stake £5, £2 and £2; £10 comes back.

byKey.ret: That is the return. Subtract the £9 staked.

explain.text: $1/2 + 1/5 + 1/5 = 9/10$, so £9 buys £10 on every outcome. The board is an arbitrage worth 1/10 of the payout. The two 4 to 1 bets are the generous ones.

items.prose: One die. A contract pays twice the face if the face is odd, and nothing if it is even.
items.question: What is it worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $2, 0, 6, 0, 10, 0$ over six faces.

byKey.odd: You averaged the odd faces only.
byKey.once: That is F, the face if odd. This pays twice as much.

explain.text: The payoffs 2, 6 and 10 total 18 over six faces: 3. It is $2F$ face by face, so its price is $2 \times 1.5$. Prices scale as payoffs do.

items.prose: Quotes: A (the face) at 3.6 to 3.8, and E (the face if even) at 1.6 to 1.8. F (the face if odd) is 1.4 to 1.5.
items.question: What is the locked profit per set, in pounds?

widget.accept: £0.30: buy E at 1.8 and F at 1.5, sell A at 3.6.
widget.label: Profit per set

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy E and F at their asks; sell A at its bid.

byKey.rev: You sold E and F and bought A. That loses.

explain.text: E and F cost $1.8 + 1.5 = 3.3$ and pay A on every face. A sells at 3.6, so £0.30 is locked. Here A is too dear for its parts.

items.prose: Two dice. A put with strike 6 pays $6 - S$ when the sum is below 6.
items.question: What is it worth? Give 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sums 2 to 5 pay 4, 3, 2, 1 on 1, 2, 3, 4 rolls.

byKey.chance: That is the chance it pays, 10/36.

explain.text: $(4 + 6 + 6 + 4)/36 = 20/36 = 5/9$. It mirrors the 8-call, which is also 5/9. Symmetry about 7 halves the work.

items.prose: The 6-put on two dice is worth $5/9$.
items.question: By parity, what is the 6-call worth? Give 4 places.

byKey.same: You set the call equal to the put. That holds only at strike 7.

explain.text: $C_6 = 5/9 + 1 = 14/9$. Below 7, calls are dearer than puts by $7 - K$. It matches the 8-put, its mirror.

items.prose: £50 bankroll. Bet 1: evens with chance 0.6. Bet 2: 2 to 1 with chance 0.5. At most £15 at risk in the round.
items.question: What do you stake on bet 2, in pounds? Give 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both Kelly stakes, then scale both by $15/22.5$.

byKey.full: That is the uncapped Kelly stake. The total, £22.50, breaks the cap.
byKey.cutone: You cut only bet 2. Scale both by the same factor.

explain.text: Kelly stakes £10 on bet 1 and $0.25 \times 50 = £12.50$ on bet 2, £22.50 in all. Scaling by $15/22.5 = 2/3$ gives £6.67 and £8.33. Equal scaling keeps the mix the same under the cap.
